issues.title: Run A: walk acceptance rows A4 through A17
issues.body:
`docs/e2e-acceptance-plan.md` stopped at A3.11 on 4 August. Ninety-nine rows remain across fourteen sections: convergence, settings, policies, the gate, rollout, the update board, remote actions, secrets, demonstrability, USB and printing, the local administrator, user rights, elevation and the release cache.

The plan itself was re-read against the code on 10 August and five checkable expectations hold (`incident.CoreGrace`, `observed.InactiveWindow`, the condition metric name, the provisional state, and the closed endpoints), so the rows can be trusted.

**Blocked on hardware.** Roughly sixty rows need a laptop that is currently powered off. A1.6 is already filled in because it needs nothing but a request from outside the cluster.

Done when every row carries an observed proof. The plan's own rule: a step with no observable proof has not been tested, even when nothing went wrong.

issues.title: Prove device login over LDAPS on a real machine
issues.body:
Audit finding H3. Staff passwords crossed the cluster network in the clear on a simple bind.

**The fleet document is done** (overlay `bd0b1b6`): `ldaps://` with the internal CA in `identity.tlsCaCert` and the plaintext acknowledgement withdrawn, so `ldap_auth_disable_tls_never_use_in_production` no longer appears in a rendered configuration. Verified with openssl using the exact PEM that ships, and the rendered CA file is byte-identical to it.

**No device has it.** Ring pins are git refs and none has been promoted. This closes on a real login over port 636 on ring 0 - a successful build proves nothing about a successful bind.

Afterwards, and only then: `olcSecurity: ssf=128` with `olcLocalSSF` on the directories. Enforcing while one device still uses port 389 locks that device out.

issues.title: Provision and retire one clean isolated cell, end to end
issues.body:
Multi-tenancy is in 1.0 scope (`docs/1.0-fit-gap.md` §5, ADR 0009). The console surface exists; what has never been done is the whole life of a cell - created, used, and removed - with the demo cell retired from the cluster afterwards.

Retirement is the half that is easy to skip and the half that matters: a tenancy model that cannot cleanly delete a tenant is one a customer cannot leave.

issues.title: Finish OpenBao: mesh route, one secret proved, precedence fix
issues.body:
ADR 0018 puts OpenBao in 1.0 as the backend for secrets classified *Revocable*. Three things are open: the mesh route to reach it from a device, one secret proved end to end on hardware, and the precedence fix - a name present in both backends must be **refused** rather than silently served from agenix.

That last one is the point. Silently preferring one backend is how a rotated secret keeps working from the wrong place and nobody notices.

Carries the ordering trap already recorded: an admin recovery path must not run through a secret that only the thing being recovered can decrypt.

issues.title: Run B: the integrations, proved from the device side
issues.body:
Section 2 of the fit-gap. A NetBird cluster routing-peer, a minimal Wazuh manager, the OpenBao mesh route, and the device-side proof of each.

Mostly platform-repo work rather than this repository, but it gates 1.0 because an integration whose console card is complete and whose device half was never observed is not an integration.

issues.title: Re-prove the gate against a change that carries a core bump
issues.body:
ADR 0020. The gate used to receive only the candidate `fleet.json`, so a change carrying anything more - a core bump in `flake.lock`, an overlay module from the ADR 0014 editor - was validated against a tree that did not contain it. Measured 6 August: a core update passed the gate, merged, and left `main` unable to evaluate for the workplace class.

The fix ships in 0.84.0 and production runs 0.86.0, so the version condition is met. **Nobody has redone the measurement that found the incident.** One deliberate run - a change carrying a `flake.lock` bump, evaluated for both device classes - before the 1.0.0 tag rather than after somebody merges a core update.

This is the safety property the product sells; it should not be taken on version numbers alone.

issues.title: Assign key management for SEXTANT_SECRET_KEY
issues.body:
The observed plane is backed up off-cluster and the restore path has been walked: counts matched and the md5 of all LUKS ciphertext came back identical on 7 August (`docs/runbooks/restore-observed-plane.md`).

That proves the backup is complete and restorable. It does **not** prove the recovery keys can be opened. That needs `SEXTANT_SECRET_KEY`, which is not in the backup and never will be, and whose management is assigned to nobody.

Without it a restore produces ciphertext no one can read, including every device's LUKS recovery key. Needs an owner and a documented escrow that the cluster's own failure cannot reach.

issues.title: Multiple drives, and stable disk addressing
issues.body:
Ref: forgejo #49.

Two disko profiles exist and both hardcode `/dev/nvme0n1`. A second drive is not partitioned, not encrypted and not wiped - so a crypto-wipe destroys the keys of one disk and leaves the other readable, which is not what anybody expects from the word "wipe".

Enumeration order is also not a promise: with two NVMe drives, "the first one" can move between boots. `/dev/disk/by-id` is the fix.

Core work, so it goes to DAWO-NixOS as a fork and a pull request.

issues.title: App profiles in the console
issues.body:
Ref: forgejo #54.

The additive model already works; what is missing is the named, reusable profile - "this group gets the design set" rather than eleven checkboxes repeated per group.

**Needs a decision first**: the boundary with the DAWO core. What stays in the image and what the console composes. Measured 10 August, that boundary is narrower than it sounds - two image-time namespaces (`secureboot.`, `diskUnlock.`) and one class distinction (`apps.*` is absent on a station). See `docs/competitive-intake.md`, "What that boundary actually is today".

issues.title: Admin devices as a named device class
issues.body:
Theme I of `docs/competitive-intake.md`, nine items, six of them value 4-5 at effort 1-2. Decided 10 August: `admin` becomes a fifth entry in the overlay's `byClass`, alongside laptop, desktop, station and server.

**The trigger has already fired.** The machine administering this fleet holds the SSH keys to the station and the forge, cluster credentials, the age identity that opens the fleet's secrets, and the object-storage credentials for the backups - and it joins the fleet as the first admin device this week, before any of these items exists.

Order: I7 (key registration as fleet data) leads because the others read from it, then I2 (an admin account that refuses to build without a registered key), I3 (`sudo` behind the token), I8 (the lockout matrix), I1 (PAM U2F), I4 (SSH via resident FIDO2) and I5 (a FIDO2 keyslot for LUKS, image-time under the existing `diskUnlock.` prefix).

The rule to hold: **two registered tokens, or a documented break-glass that is not itself protected by the thing being recovered.**

issues.title: A garbage-collection policy for devices
issues.body:
A one-day-old laptop already carried 101 dead store paths. Not a problem this year; certainly one in a fleet nobody prunes.

The policy is the work, not the command: how many generations a device keeps, how that interacts with rollback after a bad switch, and whether it is a fleet setting or a class default.

issues.title: Make the Wazuh agent useful on NixOS
issues.body:
The agent enrols and reports; most of what it then does is aimed at a distribution we are not running. Two very different causes:

**The engine works, the content is wrong.** The bundled CIS Debian policies check `dpkg` state and file modes on paths that are store symlinks, so SCA scores are noise. The FIM defaults watch an `/etc` that is a symlink tree rewritten on every generation. The active-response scripts shell out to `iptables` and to binaries not on the unit's PATH - so response fails **without failing loudly**, which is the dangerous shape. All of it is ours to fix and the policy content is reusable at the next customer.

**The data source does not exist.** Syscollector reads `dpkg`/`rpm` for its package inventory and NixOS has neither, so vulnerability detection reports a clean fleet for every device. Not fixable inside Wazuh: its matcher is fed by vendor advisory streams and nixpkgs publishes none. Answered instead by `nix run sextant#fleet-sbom`.

The inversion worth building: on NixOS the signal equivalent to "packages were installed" is a change to `/nix/var/nix/profiles/system`. One watch there, correlated with a closure diff, beats file-level FIM on a mutable distribution.

Settle first whether Wazuh 5.0 is GA and how enrolment works there - `agent-auth` is reported removed, so building on 4.x carries a known expiry.

issues.title: Per-item compliance results, and a machine-readable report per device
issues.body:
Intake A2 + G3, scheduled as one capability rather than two: they are the same thing from both ends.

Today the compliance baseline produces one aggregate verdict per device. That is not evidence an auditor can work from - they ask which control failed, on which device, measured when. Per-item results give that, and a machine-readable artifact per device under a versioned schema id is the form they ask for it in.

Trigger: the first compliance audit at a customer.

issues.title: Manual accessibility round: keyboard, screen reader, contrast, reflow
issues.body:
WCAG 2.2 AA and EN 301 549 are a legal obligation for this product.

**The mechanical half is done and held.** 73 form fields with no accessible name and 11 icon-only buttons went to zero on 7 August, and `internal/http/web/a11y_test.go` fails the build on a new one.

**The manual half has never been done and has no owner.** Keyboard order and visible focus over the five core screens, a screen reader (NVDA or VoiceOver) on the same five, contrast measured rather than eyeballed in both themes, reflow to 400%, error identification in text rather than colour, and the four new 2.2 criteria.

Until it is done the accessibility statement stays a draft. A statement claiming more than has been tested is a false declaration; "partially compliant" is the normal and expected answer.

**This needs a person, not an engineer.** Marked help wanted for exactly that reason.

issues.title: Capability RBAC on directory groups
issues.body:
Ref: forgejo #53.

Today the model is Viewer/Editor/Owner scoped by group - the right shape and too coarse. Permissions on a small set of named capabilities: start a rollout, approve a wave, wipe a device, reveal a secret, change endpoint controls, change access itself. Each bound to a directory group at a scope.

Trigger: the first customer with more than one administrator.

issues.title: Narrow four-eyes approval to where it earns its place
issues.body:
A rule rather than a list: a change the gate and the test ring can prove is fine needs no second person; a change that removes the gate, removes the ring, or removes the ability to recover needs one.

Blanket four-eyes on everything teaches people to approve without reading, which is worse than not having it - the approval becomes a signature rather than a review.

issues.title: A second remote for comin, so losing the forge does not freeze the fleet
issues.body:
Measured 10 August: a device polls exactly one remote. `services.comin.remotes` is set with `mkForce` to a single entry, and the overlay repository has no mirror. The Sextant source lives on three forges; the repository the fleet actually follows lives on one.

Losing the forge breaks nothing immediately - every device keeps running its current generation. But **nothing can be changed on any device** until a forge exists again at the same URL, and that URL lives in the repository nobody can reach. No rollout, no setting, no security fix.

The fix is small: comin's `remotes` is a list, so a second entry is configuration rather than a feature. It needs a mirror of the overlay to exist first, which it does not.

Recorded as an accepted risk in `docs/runbooks/disaster-recovery.md` until then.

issues.title: OCSF audit sink
issues.body:
Intake A4. Value 4 at effort 2, and unscheduled because its trigger has not fired: nobody has yet asked to ingest our audit trail into their SIEM.

The work is the class mapping rather than the transport - 6003 API activity, 3002 account change, 1001 file activity - and it is directly reusable.

Cheap and valuable is a reason to do it quickly **when asked**, not a reason to do it now. Filed so the answer to "does it integrate with our SIEM" is "here is the issue" rather than "no".

issues.title: Versioned config export envelope that refuses unknown types
issues.body:
Intake G2. An export wrapped in a versioned envelope that **refuses** to import a type this build does not know, rather than silently dropping it.

Silently dropping is how an import looks successful and produces a fleet missing a policy nobody notices is gone.

Unscheduled: the trigger is the first consumer of an export that is not us. It matters for the exit question a municipality asks - can we leave, and does what we take with us still mean anything.

issues.title: Measure the memory a device needs during nixos-rebuild
issues.body:
`docs/architecture/scale.md` carries real measurements, and this is the gap in them: how much memory a device needs while converging.

It matters because it is what a customer buys. And it stops being academic if the binary cache is unavailable - devices then build the closure themselves rather than substituting it.

Measurable on one existing machine, no fleet required:

```
systemd-run --unit=c5 --remain-after-exit -p MemoryAccounting=yes \
  nixos-rebuild switch --flake <ref>
systemctl show c5.service -p MemoryPeak
```

If `MemoryPeak` is empty on an older systemd, read `memory.peak` from the unit's cgroup before stopping it. Report the number with the device class and whether the cache was reachable.

issues.title: Managed local administrator credentials, the way LUKS keys already are
issues.body:
Sextant escrows a device's LUKS recovery key: stored sealed, revealed through the console, every reveal in the audit log. It does none of that for the **local administrator password**, which is the credential an operator actually reaches for when a device will not let them in.

Today `dawo.localAdmin.passwordSecret` names a secret holding a **yescrypt hash**, which the device consumes and nobody can read back. The plaintext lives wherever the operator put it, or nowhere.

**Found the hard way on 2026-08-10.** Before promoting a login-transport change to a ring, the break-glass account for that ring was checked. The account exists, its key-based SSH works, and its password is recorded in no vault, no document and no secret. The fallback was real only because a shared bootstrap account with a documented password still exists - itself an audit finding, and the thing the local admin was meant to replace.

**Intune does this better and it is worth saying so.** Windows LAPS rotates the local administrator password, escrows it, and audits every reveal. We have the machinery for exactly this pattern and point it at disk-encryption keys only.

Done when:

- the console can generate a local administrator password, store it sealed, and reveal it with an audit entry - the same path recovery keys take
- rotation is a console action rather than a commit, since the device consumes a hash and a new hash is a new generation
- the reveal is scoped like other secrets, so it is not a fleet-wide capability
- and the bootstrap account can finally be turned off, which today would remove the only recovery path anybody can prove

That last point is the reason this is not cosmetic. The migration the module documents - turn on localAdmin, prove login and sudo, then disable the shared bootstrap account - cannot be completed while nobody holds the replacement credential.

Belongs with the lockout matrix in the admin-devices work: four uses, four recovery paths, and no path protected by the thing it recovers.

issues.title: Console: a stale comin failure flag reads as a broken device
issues.body:
comin's `comin_last_eval_failed`, `comin_last_build_failed` and friends are **sticky**. Measured on the station on 11 August: half an hour after a broken ring had been reverted and the machine had deployed cleanly, `comin_last_eval_failed` was still `1`, alongside `comin_deployment_info{status="done"}` for the current commit and 324 successful fetches.

The flag records the last evaluation that *ran*. A poll with nothing new to evaluate does not clear it, so the flag survives until the next real evaluation - which on a settled fleet may be days.

The agent (`agent/src/collect.rs`) now says "last evaluation failed" rather than implying the present tense, because it cannot tell a stale flag from a live one: that needs the target revision, and the device does not have it. Note that deployment status cannot date the flag either - in the captured reading the deployment succeeded and the flag was still set.

**The console can decide it, and should.** It holds the ring's target revision and the device's reported revision. A device on target with a set flag is reporting history; a device behind target with a set flag is reporting the reason it is behind. Those should not look the same on the device page.

Fixture with the real reading: `agent/tests/fixtures/comin-metrics-stale-flag.txt`. Test: `a_stale_eval_flag_is_reported_as_the_last_evaluation_not_the_current_state`.

issues.title: Console can only bump the core input, so gate item 6 waits on upstream
issues.body:
`cmd/sextant/capabilities.go:442` wires the update board's bump with a literal input name:

```go
up.WithDelivery(rg.BumpInput, d.changes.EditFile, d.changes.Submit, "dawo")
```

The gate-runner's `/bump` endpoint takes the input name from the request body and can bump any of them. The console can bump one.

Measured on the bb-open overlay on 11 August: of fourteen flake inputs, twelve follow `dawo`. Only `dawo` and `sextant` are independently pinned. So the only flake.lock bump the console can produce is the core update.

**Why this blocks something.** Gate item 6 and acceptance section A7 both need a change that carries a flake.lock bump, judged by the gate against the core it names. The console's own path produces exactly one such change, and today approving it is a regression: the fleet pins `dawo` at `f250cd4c1162`, which exists only on the fork branch `feat/printing-driver-set-and-discovery`, so the update would remove `feat(printing): name the driver set, and let discovery be turned off` and return ten lines of README.

Once that commit lands on the core's main (now public as https://codeberg.org/DAWO/DAWO-Core), the core update becomes a genuine step forward and A7 is one approval in the console.

**The decision this needs.** Whether the bump input stays hardcoded. Arguments for leaving it: core updates are the only bump with a watcher, a supersede rule and a queue behind them, and widening it invites a menu nobody asked for. Arguments against: the overlay's `sextant` pin also moves, nothing offers it, and it is bumped by hand today.

Not urgent for 1.0 beyond recording it, because the upstream PR resolves the immediate block either way.
